idea_angle: A roundup of the seven scams that hit in the weeks after the holidays, when people return, resell, set up and pay off gifts.

script.title: 7 scams that hit after the holidays (returns, resales and new gadgets)
script.hook: 7 scams wait for you after the holidays, when you return, resell and set up gifts. Here's each one, and its fix.

segments.heading: Why late December
segments.narration: The week after the holidays feels like the danger's over. The shopping's done. But this is when we return things, resell what we didn't want, set up new gadgets, and look at our bank statements. Scammers follow every one of those habits. So here are the seven scams that hit between Christmas and the end of January, with how each one works, the tell, and the fix. And at the end, one habit that beats all seven.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes sitting among opened gift boxes No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1. Refund texts
segments.narration: Number one, the fake refund text. You return something on Monday, and on Tuesday a text says your refund is on hold, confirm your card to receive it. The link copies the store's look and takes your card details. The tell: real refunds go back to the card or account you paid with, automatically. Nobody needs your card number again. The fix: check refunds in the store's own app, the website you type yourself, or your card statement. Forward fake texts to seven seven two six.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a refund text and a hook No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 2. The code buyer
segments.narration: Number two, the buyer who wants a code. You list an unwanted gift, and a buyer says they need to make sure you're real. 'I'll text you a code, read it back to me.' That code lets them create a phone number in your name or get into one of your accounts. The tell: a buyer has no reason to need anything from your phone. The fix: codes stay on your phone, always. If you already shared one, change that account's password and turn on two-step sign-in.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a six-digit code and a reaching hand No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 3. Fake payment emails
segments.narration: Number three, the fake payment email. The buyer says they've paid, and an email that looks like your payment app says three hundred dollars received, on hold until you upgrade to a business account. Then the buyer asks you to send the fee, or refund an 'overpayment'. The tell: money that isn't in your balance hasn't been paid, and receiving a personal payment shouldn't cost a fee. The fix: open your payment app or bank yourself and check. No money, no sale.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an email with a pending stamp No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 4. Activation sites
segments.narration: Number four, fake activation sites. Your new streaming stick or smart TV shows an address and a code. If you search 'activate' instead of typing the address, some results are look-alike sites that charge ninety-nine dollars or want to connect to your computer. The tell: any charge or remote access to activate. The fix: type the exact address on your TV. Activation is free. If you're setting up a parent's device, do it with them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a TV with a code and a fake help window No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 5. Free trials
segments.narration: Number five, free trial traps. New Year resolution ads offer a free supplement or fitness program, just pay shipping. In the small print, the trial becomes a monthly charge, often eighty or ninety dollars. Sometimes the ad uses a fake news story with a celebrity who never endorsed it. The fix: before you pay shipping, find the price after the trial and how to cancel. Already charged? Cancel in writing, then dispute it with your card issuer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a gift box with a long receipt No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 6. Balance checks
segments.narration: Number six, fake gift card balance sites. You search 'check gift card balance' and land on a look-alike site that asks for the card number and PIN. A moment later, the balance is gone. The tell: you found the site through a search ad, not the address on the back of the card. The fix: check balances only on the website or phone number printed on the card itself, or at the store's register. And use gift cards soon; the longer they sit, the longer someone has to drain them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a gift card with a search bar and a mask No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 7. Unclaimed money
segments.narration: Number seven, unclaimed money texts. 'You have one thousand two hundred forty-seven dollars in unclaimed funds. Pay a forty-nine dollar fee to release it.' Unclaimed money is real, which is why the scam works. But searching and claiming through your state's official program is free. The fix: go to USA dot gov slash unclaimed money, which links to every state's official site. Search your name and old addresses, and your parents' names too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a treasure chest with a price tag on the lock No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The one habit
segments.narration: So here's the one habit that beats all seven: go to the source yourself. The store's own app for refunds. Your own payment app for payments. The address on the TV for activation. The back of the card for balances. The state's own site for unclaimed money. Never the link, the email, or the search ad. Save this video, send it to whoever's handling returns in your house, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

idea_angle: A New Year money cleanup: find every recurring charge, spot ones you never signed up for, cancel safely, and set up alerts so trial traps and fraud can't hide.

script.title: Find and cancel every subscription you forgot (a 30-minute New Year cleanup)
script.hook: 30 minutes, 3 places to look, and every recurring charge you forgot. Here's the New Year subscription cleanup.

segments.heading: Why January
segments.narration: January is when free trials from December turn into charges, annual renewals hit, and anyone who stole a card number over the holidays starts testing it. It's also when most of us are already looking at our money. So this is a thirty-minute cleanup. Three places to look, one kind of charge that means fraud, how to cancel without getting scammed while you do it, and the alerts that make sure nothing hides again. Grab your last two months of statements and let's go.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes with a stopwatch and a stack of statements No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Place 1: statements
segments.narration: Place one, your card and bank statements. Go back two months, because some things bill every other month or quarterly. Highlight every charge that repeats, and every name you don't recognise. Write each one down with its amount. Billing names can be strange, like a parent company instead of the product, so search the name before you panic. Most people find at least one thing they forgot. Some find several, and it adds up to hundreds a year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a statement with highlighted lines No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Place 2: app stores
segments.narration: Place two, your phone's app store subscriptions. On most phones it's in your account settings, under subscriptions. These don't always show clearly on your card statement, because they're billed through the app store. Look for apps you haven't opened in months, and free trials that quietly became paid. Cancel them there. Deleting an app doesn't cancel its subscription. That one catches a lot of people.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone settings screen with a subscriptions list No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Place 3: email
segments.narration: Place three, your email. Search for words like receipt, renewal, subscription and trial. You'll find sign-ups you forgot, and the cancellation instructions too. While you're there, notice any 'your subscription has renewed' emails for things you never had. Those are often fake invoice scams. Never call the number in them. Check your real statement instead. If the charge isn't there, the email is fake.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an inbox with a search bar No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Test charges
segments.narration: Now the charge that matters most: small, unfamiliar amounts, like one dollar, two ninety-nine, or a charity donation you didn't make. Thieves often test a stolen card with a small charge before a big one. If you see one, don't wait to see what happens. Call the number on the back of your card, report it, and ask for a new card number. Under federal law, your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is limited, especially when you report quickly.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a tiny charge with a magnifying glass No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Cancel safely
segments.narration: Cancelling has its own traps. Only cancel through the company's website or app, typed in yourself, or the app store. Don't search 'cancel' plus the company name and call the first number, because fake support lines advertise there. If a company makes cancelling hard, cancel in writing, keep a copy, and then ask your card issuer to dispute any later charges. A real company will never ask for remote access to your computer to cancel.
segments.on_screen_text: Cancel via the real site or app
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a cancel button with a shield No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Set alerts
segments.narration: Last step, so nothing hides again. Turn on alerts for every transaction, on every card and account, in your bank's app. It feels like a lot of notifications. That's the point: you'll see a free trial turn paid, a test charge, or a renewal the moment it happens. Then put a reminder in your calendar for next January to do this again. Thirty minutes once a year, and you'll catch both the forgotten subscriptions and the fraud.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a notification bell No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Tax season scams 2027: 8 to know before you file
script.hook: 8 tax scams run from January to April. Here's every one, plus the 6-digit PIN that stops the worst of them.

segments.heading: Why tax season
segments.narration: Tax season puts more money in motion than any other time of year: refunds, payments, and millions of documents with Social Security numbers on them. That makes it the busiest season for scams that copy the IRS, tax preparers and payroll. Here are the eight that run from January to April. For each one you'll get how it works and the rule that exposes it. And stay for the end, because one free six-digit number stops the most expensive of them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes next to a stack of tax forms and a calendar No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1. IRS texts
segments.narration: Number one, fake IRS texts and emails. 'Your refund is ready, verify your identity,' with a link that copies the IRS site. The rule: the IRS doesn't start contact by text, email or social media to ask for personal or financial information. It usually starts with a letter. Check anything at IRS dot gov, typed in yourself. Forward fake texts to seven seven two six and fake emails to phishing at IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a fake seal No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 2. IRS calls
segments.narration: Number two, the threatening call. 'You owe back taxes. Pay today with gift cards or a wire, or police will come.' The caller ID may even say IRS. The rule: the IRS doesn't demand immediate payment by gift card, wire or crypto, and it doesn't threaten arrest or deportation. You'll get a letter and a chance to question what you owe. Hang up and report the call to the Treasury Inspector General at TIGTA dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a badge and a gift card No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 3. Ghost preparers
segments.narration: Number three, ghost preparers. They charge you to prepare your return, then won't sign it or include a preparer tax ID. Their fee is often a cut of your refund, and some send the refund to their own account. If anything's wrong, the IRS comes to you, not them. The rule: paid preparers must sign and include their PTIN. Get a signed copy, read it before you sign, and make sure the refund goes to your account.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an unsigned form with a see-through figure No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 4. Tax hacks
segments.narration: Number four, social media tax hacks. Videos promise a secret refund: a fuel credit meant for farm equipment, sick leave credits for twenty twenty and twenty twenty-one, or made-up wages on a W-2. The IRS has warned about all of these. It can freeze the refund, ask for it back with interest, and add penalties, including five thousand dollars for a frivolous return. The rule: if everyone qualifies, it isn't a secret. Look it up on IRS dot gov first.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone video with a penalty envelope No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 5. W-2 phishing
segments.narration: Number five, W-2 phishing. Employees get 'your W-2 is ready, log in' emails that copy their payroll login. Payroll staff get emails that look like the CEO, asking for every employee's W-2. Either way, a W-2 gives a thief everything needed for a fake return. The rule: open payroll from a bookmark or the app, and if you work in HR, call to confirm any W-2 request, even from the top.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an email with a payroll login and a hook No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 6. Refund theft
segments.narration: Number six, refund theft. With a Social Security number from a data breach, a thief files early, with made-up income, and the refund goes to their account. You find out when your e-filed return is rejected. The fix: file on paper anyway, attach Form fourteen oh three nine if the IRS instructions say so, report at IdentityTheft dot gov, and freeze your credit. Expect it to take months.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a rejected stamp on a tax form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 7. Fake free filing
segments.narration: Number seven, fake free filing. Searching 'free tax filing' brings up ads. Some are real products with upsells, and some are look-alike sites collecting Social Security numbers. Free filing is real: IRS Free File for people under the income limit, and VITA and TCE volunteers who prepare returns for free. The rule: start at IRS dot gov and follow its links, never an ad.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a search ad with a mask No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 8. Refund letters
segments.narration: Number eight, the 'you're owed a refund' letter or text that asks for a fee or your bank login to release it. Sometimes it claims to be about a stimulus payment or a tax credit. The rule: the IRS doesn't charge fees to send you your refund, and you can check any refund yourself with the Where's My Refund tool at IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an envelope with a fee tag No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The IP PIN
segments.narration: Now the six digits. An IRS Identity Protection PIN is a free number, new each year, that only you and the IRS know. Once you have one, any return filed with your Social Security number has to include it, so a thief can't file in your name. Anyone with a Social Security number or taxpayer ID can get one through their IRS online account. Do it in January, before filing opens. Save this video, send it to whoever does the taxes in your house, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

script.title: How to file your taxes safely: documents, preparers and protecting your refund
script.hook: 5 steps from W-2 to refund, and at each one, the scam to watch for. How to file your taxes safely.

segments.heading: The five steps
segments.narration: Filing taxes has five steps: lock down your account, gather documents, choose how to file, file and check, and get your refund. At every one of those steps there's a scam built to meet you. So let's walk through them in order, with the protection for each. None of this needs special software, and most of it is free.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes next to five stepping stones No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: lock it
segments.narration: Step one, before anything else: get an IRS Identity Protection PIN. Create or sign in to your IRS online account at IRS dot gov, and request one. It's free and changes each year. With it, nobody can file a return using your Social Security number. While you're there, check your account for anything odd. And freeze your credit at the three bureaus if you haven't already. The scam to watch for: emails offering to 'help you set up your IRS account'. Do it yourself, from IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a PIN padlock on a tax form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: documents
segments.narration: Step two, gather your documents: W-2s from employers, 1099s for freelance work, interest and investments, and forms for things like mortgage interest or tuition. Most arrive by the end of January or mid-February. The scam: 'your W-2 is ready' or 'your 1099 is available' emails that copy payroll and bank logins. Get every document from the website or app you open yourself, never from an email link. And keep paper copies somewhere safe, because they're a thief's favourite documents.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a folder of forms and a bookmark icon No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: choose
segments.narration: Step three, choose how to file. If your income is under the limit, IRS Free File offers free guided software, and VITA and TCE volunteers will prepare it for free. Start from IRS dot gov to find both, not a search ad. If you use a paid preparer, check four things: they have a PTIN, they'll sign the return, their fee isn't a cut of your refund, and the refund goes to your account. The scam: ghost preparers and social media 'refund experts' who promise more than anyone else.
segments.on_screen_text: 3. Free option or a real preparer
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. two paths: a free sign and a signed form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: file and check
segments.narration: Step four, file, and check before you sign. Read the return. Is your income right? Are the credits ones you actually qualify for? Is your bank account number correct? If a preparer added something you don't understand, ask. You're legally responsible for everything on it. The scam to watch for: credits pushed by viral videos, like fuel tax credits or old sick leave credits. If you're unsure, look up the credit on IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a magnifying glass over a form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 5: the refund
segments.narration: Step five, the refund. Choose direct deposit to an account in your name. Track it with the Where's My Refund tool on IRS dot gov, typed in yourself. The scams: texts saying your refund is on hold until you verify, calls offering to speed it up for a fee, and 'refund advance' offers with hidden costs. The IRS doesn't charge fees to send your refund, and it doesn't text you about it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a refund check going into a bank No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: After you file
segments.narration: After you file, keep a copy of the return and your documents. The IRS generally recommends keeping records for at least three years. Shred old paper documents you no longer need, rather than throwing them out. And if a letter from the IRS arrives later, check it against your online account before you call anyone, using the number on IRS dot gov, not the letter's if you're unsure.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a filing box and a shredder No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Wrap
segments.narration: So: lock your account, get documents from the source, choose a free option or a real preparer, read before you sign, and track your refund yourself. Five steps, five protections. Save this for when your W-2 arrives, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

script.title: How a wrong-number text becomes a $100,000 loss (crypto investment scams explained)
script.hook: 1 wrong-number text, 6 stages, and a $100,000 loss. Here's how crypto investment scams work, and the exit at every stage.

segments.heading: The text
segments.narration: 'Hi, is this Amy? Are we still on for dinner Thursday?' You reply, sorry, wrong number. They apologise, compliment your profile picture, and ask how your week's going. This is how one of the most expensive scams in the world starts. The FBI counts losses to crypto investment fraud in the billions of dollars a year. Today we'll follow a fictional composite we'll call Mark, through six stages, from that text to a total loss. And at every stage, the exit he could have taken.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes looking at a phone with a friendly wrong-number text No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Stage 1: contact
segments.narration: Stage one, contact. The first message is a mistake that isn't a mistake: a wrong number, a dating match, a friendly comment on social media. The person is warm, successful, and in no hurry. They don't ask for anything. They just keep talking. The exit: a stranger who turns a wrong number into a daily conversation is a pattern, not luck. You don't have to be rude. You just don't have to reply.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a wrong-number bubble No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Stage 2: friendship
segments.narration: Stage two, friendship. For weeks, sometimes months, they message every day. Good morning photos, meals, a nice car, a life story with some sadness in it. They ask about yours and remember the details. They often suggest moving to a private chat app. Mark comes to look forward to these messages. The exit: you've never met, never had a real call, and you know a lot less about them than they know about you.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a stack of good morning messages No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Stage 3: the tip
segments.narration: Stage three, the tip. Casually, they mention how they afford their life: an uncle who trades, a special crypto platform, a strategy that never loses. They don't push. They let you ask. Then they offer to show you, step by step, and send a link to an app or website. The exit: investment advice from someone you've only met online is the turning point. Check the platform at Investor dot gov and FINRA BrokerCheck, and search its name plus 'scam'.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a chat bubble with a chart No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Stage 4: the proof
segments.narration: Stage four, the proof. Mark puts in two thousand dollars, and the balance climbs fast. He even withdraws three hundred, and it arrives. That small withdrawal is on purpose. Over the next month, he puts in savings, then a retirement withdrawal, then a loan. The screen says he's up to a hundred and forty thousand. The exit: the platform controls the number on that screen. A small payout proves nothing. The real test is withdrawing most of it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a rising chart and a tiny coin No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Stage 5: the wall
segments.narration: Stage five, the wall. Mark tries to withdraw. 'Account flagged. Pay twenty percent tax before release.' Then an 'anti-money laundering deposit'. Then a 'late fee'. His friend urges him to pay, and even offers to cover part of it. The exit is here, even this late: any fee to withdraw means the balance was never real. Stop paying. Save every message, wallet address and transaction, and report it at I-C-3 dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a brick wall made of fee tags No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Stage 6: second scam
segments.narration: Stage six, the second scam. Weeks later, Mark gets a message: a recovery firm, or someone claiming to be from a government agency, can get his money back for an upfront fee. They know exactly what he lost, because scammers share victim lists. The exit: government agencies don't charge you to recover money, and nobody can trace crypto back for a fee. Report for free, talk to your bank, and block anyone offering recovery.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. three masks and a fee tag No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Helping someone
segments.narration: If this is happening to someone you love, they may not believe you at first. They've been told family won't understand. Ask questions instead of lecturing: how did you meet, have you met in person, have you tried withdrawing most of it? Offer to look up the platform together. If money's gone, say it's not their fault, because these are organised professionals. Then call the bank together and report at I-C-3 dot gov. script.title: Romance scams before Valentine's: how to spot one, and how to help someone in one
script.hook: 1 money question beats every romance scam, even the ones with AI video calls. Here's the full guide before Valentine's.

segments.heading: Why February
segments.narration: Romance scams run all year, but the weeks before Valentine's Day are when loneliness feels loudest and dating apps are busiest. The FTC reports people lose over a billion dollars a year to romance scams, and those are only the ones reported. Today: where scammers find people, what the profile looks like, the new AI tricks, the money stories, and the one question that beats all of it. Then, how to help someone you love who's already in one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes holding a heart in front of a calendar showing February No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where they find you
segments.narration: Dating apps, of course, but also social media comments, friend requests, games with chat, groups for widows or hobbies, and wrong-number texts. Scammers look for people who are recently divorced or widowed, or who post about being lonely or retired. They don't need you to be naive. They need you to be human, and to have some time.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a map of chat bubbles across different apps No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The profile
segments.narration: The profile is attractive but not too perfect. Usually a job that keeps them far away: deployed military, an engineer on an oil rig or ship, a doctor with an aid group abroad. The photos are stolen from real people, or now generated by AI. A reverse image search often finds the same face under another name. No match doesn't prove they're real, though, because AI-made faces won't show up anywhere else.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a profile card with a faraway icon No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Moving off the app
segments.narration: Within days, they ask to move to a private chat app: 'I'm hardly on here.' That's because dating apps can spot and remove scam accounts. Then the pace picks up. Messages every morning and night, early 'I love you's, plans for a future together. Scammers often work from scripts, sometimes in teams. A good reply filters many of them: 'I'd like to keep chatting here until we meet.'
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a heart moving from one app to another No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Video and AI
segments.narration: The old advice was: make them video call. Still useful, since many will make excuses. But real-time face-swap tools can now put a different face on a live call, and the FBI has warned about criminals using AI-generated video. Watch for calls that are short, dark or glitchy, or that freeze when you ask them to turn their head. But don't rely on video as proof. There's a better test.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a video window with a face slipping No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The money stories
segments.narration: Eventually there's money. A flight home that their frozen account can't cover. Customs fees on equipment, or on a gift they sent you. A medical bill. Or the newest version: no request at all, just an investment platform they'd love to share with you. Payment is almost always in ways that are hard to reverse: gift cards, wires, crypto, payment apps. Each request is small at first, and each one makes the next easier.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a ladder of payment tags No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The one question
segments.narration: Here's the question that beats all of it, AI or not: have I met this person in person, and are they asking for money, or for me to invest? If the answer is no and yes, stop. No real partner you've never met needs your savings. You can say it kindly: 'I don't send money to people I haven't met.' Watch how they react. Someone real is disappointed. A scammer gets angry, desperate, or more loving than ever.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. two question cards and a stop sign No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Helping someone
segments.narration: If it's someone you love, don't start with 'that's a scam'. They've been told family won't understand, and shame pushes people closer to the scammer. Ask: tell me about them, have you met, has money come up? Offer to look at the photos together. If money's gone, say 'it's not your fault, these are professionals,' then call the bank together, report at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov, and for anyone sixty or older, call the Elder Fraud Hotline at one eight three three, FRAUD eleven. Save this, send it to someone who's dating online, and follow for one scam decoded every day.
